title: Cybersecurity Reference
description: A quick reminder of the ideas and examples in the Cybersecurity Fundamentals lessons. Open the linked lesson when you need more help.

entries.name: Protect information
entries.summary: Security includes keeping information private, correct and available when needed. These three goals are often called confidentiality, integrity and availability.

example.code:
Private: only the teacher sees a private note
Correct: a score is not changed by accident
Available: the lesson page opens when needed

notes: Protecting privacy alone does not guarantee a service remains usable or correct.

entries.name: Think about the thing you protect
entries.summary: An asset is something valuable, such as a file or saved work. A threat is something that might harm it. A risk considers how likely and harmful that problem is.

example.code:
Asset: a class project file
Threat: accidental deletion
Control: a tested backup copy

notes: Do not start with a tool before naming the problem it should reduce.

entries.name: Use strong unique passwords
entries.summary: A unique password is used for only one account. A password manager can create and remember long passwords so one leak does not unlock many accounts.

example.code:
Account A: its own long password
Account B: a different long password
Password manager: stores them in its protected vault

notes: A password written as an example in public is not a password to use.

entries.name: Add another sign-in factor
entries.summary: Multi-factor authentication asks for more than one kind of proof. A security key or an authenticator can add protection beyond a password.

example.code:
Something you know: password
Something you have: security key
Two factors protect one sign-in

notes: Never share a one-time code with someone who contacts you unexpectedly.

entries.name: Spot suspicious messages
entries.summary: Phishing is a trick that tries to make someone reveal information or take a harmful action. Pause when a message pressures you to act quickly.

example.code:
Message: Your school files vanish in 5 minutes! Send your password now.
Safer response: do not reply; contact the school through a known channel.

notes: A familiar logo or display name does not prove who sent a message.

entries.name: Check the actual address
entries.summary: A link label can differ from its destination. Read the real host name carefully before entering private information.

example.code:
Label shown: School portal
Actual host: school.example.attacker.test
Domain controlled here: attacker.test

notes: A padlock means an encrypted connection, not that the website is honest.

entries.name: Keep software updated
entries.summary: Updates often fix known weaknesses as well as ordinary bugs. Install them through the software's trusted update route.

example.code:
Known issue discovered
Maker publishes a fix
You update and restart when required

notes: Do not install an update from an unexpected message attachment.

entries.name: Give only needed access
entries.summary: Least privilege means giving each person or program only the access needed for its job. This limits damage from mistakes or misuse.

example.code:
Reader: can view lesson files
Editor: can change lesson text
Publisher: can release a reviewed version

notes: Do not give administrator access merely because it is easier to set up.

entries.name: Treat text as text
entries.summary: User-supplied text should not become executable page code by accident. textContent places text into a page without treating it as HTML.
notes: Do not put untrusted text into innerHTML. Choose a safe text API when you need text.

entries.name: Validate at a trusted boundary
entries.summary: Validation checks that data follows a rule. Browser checks help the user, but a real backend must check received data too because browser code can be changed.

example.code:
Page rule: quantity must be a whole number from 1 to 5
Backend rule in a real service: check the same limits before saving
This tutorial app: has no backend or accounts

notes: Do not trust a value just because a browser form accepted it.

entries.name: Back up and practise recovery
entries.summary: A backup is another copy of important data. A useful backup must be readable and restorable, not merely present.

example.code:
Working file: project.txt
Backup copy: stored separately
Recovery practice: open a copy and check the contents

notes: A copy on the same failing disk may be lost with the original.

entries.name: Respond calmly to a problem
entries.summary: An incident is an event that may harm security. Stop risky actions, preserve useful facts and get help from the responsible person.

example.code:
Unexpected sign-in notice
1. Do not follow the message link
2. Open the service through a known address
3. Review activity and contact its support if needed

notes: Do not erase useful evidence or accuse someone before the facts are checked.
